title: Legal wording once intimidated me. Now, it's becoming a language I can explain

blocks.text: Canada·First Person

Adu Asare remembers what it felt like to sign a legal document without fully understanding what it meant. Now he's studying to be a paralegal, hoping to help those in his Ghanaian community make sense of legal and government documents.
As I study to be a paralegal, I’m gaining knowledge and confidence to help others navigate the law
This First Person article is the experience of Adu Asare, who lives in Scarborough, Ont. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.
Two years after I arrived in Canada, I found myself holding a piece of paper containing legal jargon I did not understand.
Of course, I had questions. But I felt uncomfortable asking them.
So after the lawyer meant to help me with my Workplace Safety and Insurance Board Benefits asked me, I signed the document — without fully knowing its financial implications.
The document mentioned a contingency fee, which dictated my lawyer would retain a percentage of any settlement.

Now, I’m a paralegal student; at school, I’ve learned about contingency fees and the rest of what I was being asked to sign. But the experience in May 2023 taught me something else: that I want to help others make sense of the law.
A struggle for answers
My challenges with legal language began in my home country of Ghana.

Asare grew up in Ghana and immigrated to Canada in 2021. He had to navigate the legal paperwork of an asylum claim, seeking protection from threats, discrimination and the risk of harm if he returned to his home country. (Submitted by Adu Asare)

There, in 2019, I hired a lawyer to help with my divorce. I asked them questions, such as: What documents do I need to file? What are the legal grounds for divorce? How long will the process take? What are my rights and financial responsibilities?
The answers were often very technical, and I struggled to understand the practical implications and what I needed to do.

I faced that same sense of uncertainty when I immigrated to Canada in 2021 and had to navigate the legal paperwork of an asylum claim. I sought protection from threats to my safety, discrimination and the risk of harm if I returned to my home country.
I relied on an immigration consultant for help with my documents who, at times, did not offer the clarity I needed. That confusion made the process even more overwhelming.
How these experiences shaped me

These instances showed me that having access to a legal professional does not mean that a client feels comfortable asking questions or can make decisions with confidence — and that it can be even harder to know your legal rights when, like with my workplace accident, you are already going through a difficult time. I decided to learn about the law so that I can help others navigate legal challenges and make legal information easier to understand.

In January 2025, I enrolled in Centennial College’s Paralegal Court and Tribunal Agent program in Toronto. Learning the terminology did not change what happened in 2023, but it helped give me the confidence to ask questions.
It’s where I began to see that knowing legal terminology and explaining it clearly are two different skills. Plain language can help close that gap.
Asare is shown here in class at Centennial College. (Submitted by Adu Asare)

I put what I am learning into practice in my Ghanaian community. On one occasion, I helped someone understand an Ontario Works letter explaining that their assistance had stopped after they failed to tell their caseworker they had started a job. I have also helped people understand lawyers’ retainer agreements, sometimes explaining information in Twi, a dialect of our Akan language spoken in Ghana.

These conversations have shown me how everyday language can be used to help someone understand what a document says, and I always let them know that they can ask me any questions. Right now, I see my role as helping people understand the paperwork in front of them and to help them recognize when they need further assistance. (I am a student, not a licensed paralegal, and I know that explaining information in plain language is not a substitute for qualified legal advice.)
And I hope that by writing about legal issues, like in this essay, I can make the law and legal documents more accessible.

I am still learning how to communicate legal information accurately and responsibly. What I do know is that making the law easier to understand does not mean promising outcomes or pretending every issue has a simple answer. When I think about the person who signed that agreement in 2023, I do not see someone who lacked intelligence, I see someone trying to navigate an unfamiliar process without feeling equipped to ask the right questions.
Asare wants people to know they do not have to pretend to understand a document simply because they are afraid to ask questions. (Submitted by Adu Asare)

Looking back, I wish I had asked how the lawyer's fees would be calculated, what percentage would be deducted from any settlement and what services the agreement covered. I also wish I had asked whether the agreement could be explained to me in plain language before I signed it
I cannot change what I did not understand then. But I can use what I am learning now to help make the next person’s experience less confusing.

I want people to know they do not have to pretend to understand a document simply because they are afraid to ask. Sometimes, the first step toward making an informed decision is being able to say, “Can you explain that to me?” — and waiting for the thoughtful answer you deserve.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Adu Asare is a paralegal court and tribunal agent student at Centennial College. His interests include legal research and public legal education, with a focus on making legal information easier to understand and advancing access to justice.
